analysis.one_liner: Bans all organophosphate pesticides from food, extending the chlorpyrifos ban to the whole class.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2023 with five Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The BAN OPs From Our Food Act would amend federal food safety law so that any food containing an organophosphate pesticide — including residues and breakdown products — would be legally considered adulterated, regardless of any allowable limit set by the EPA [S3]. Organophosphates are nerve-agent-related chemicals that attack the nervous system. The bill would extend to the entire class the ban the EPA already placed on chlorpyrifos, the best-known organophosphate, from food in February 2022 [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Food consumers, especially young children whose developing nervous systems are most vulnerable to organophosphate exposure, and farmworkers and rural residents who face the heaviest exposure to these pesticides. Public health groups have long pushed for a class-wide ban because organophosphates are linked to neurodevelopmental harm even at low levels.

how_it_helps.text: Makes any food containing an organophosphate pesticide or its breakdown products legally adulterated, overriding any tolerance or exemption the EPA had set under section 408 of the food safety law [S3].
Extends to all organophosphates the approach the EPA already took with chlorpyrifos, which it banned from food in February 2022 [S2].
Places the ban in statute rather than regulation, so it could not be reversed by a future administration changing EPA policy.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of organophosphate pesticides would lose a market, and growers of crops where these chemicals are still used would lose a cheap pest-control tool, with possible costs passed to consumers. The EPA would lose some flexibility to set crop-by-crop tolerance levels.

drawbacks.text: The bill's blanket ban disregards EPA tolerances — the residue limits the agency sets for each pesticide and crop — removing case-by-case risk assessment and forbidding any use even where the EPA judged residues safe [S3].

Growers would lose a class of inexpensive, broad-spectrum insecticides; if substitutes cost more or work less well, some of that cost could show up in food prices, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: organophosphates are neurotoxic, the EPA itself already banned the class's flagship product from food, and children are especially vulnerable [S2]. The main cost is to growers who lose a cheap pest-control tool and may face higher input costs. The blunt, class-wide approach trades away EPA's crop-by-carp flexibility for a clear bright-line rule.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, moved to its Health Subcommittee four days later, and never advanced further before the Congress ended, so no committee vote and no floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on September 18, 2023, joined by Reps. Bowman, Meng, Schakowsky, and Barragan as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce; on September 22, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action was recorded, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of organophosphate pesticides and growers still using them benefit from the status quo, since no ban was enacted and the class remains regulated only through EPA tolerances.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and growers still using them

for.name: Rep. Nydia M. Velazquez
for.role: Sponsor, introduced the bill in the House
for.what_they_did: Introduced the BAN OPs From Our Food Act and recruited five original cosponsors

for.name: Reps. Jamaal Bowman, Grace Meng, Jan Schakowsky, and Nanette Barragan
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over food safety
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or moved the bill after it was referred, leaving it at the Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats [S4]; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists beyond the bill's all-Democratic sponsorship.

industries.note: A statutory ban would end sales of organophosphate products for food uses, including residues and degradation products [S3]. The industry benefits from the bill's failure, since its products remain legal subject to EPA tolerances.

Growers would lose a class of cheap, broad-spectrum insecticides; the bill removes any crop-by-crop flexibility the EPA tolerances allowed [S3]. Their interest in keeping the tools runs against the food-safety interest of consumers in this bill.

industries.industry: Producers of alternative pest controls (organic growers, biopesticide makers)
industries.note: A class-wide ban would push growers toward alternative pest-control products, expanding demand for substitutes whose use leaves no organophosphate residue.
